content.text: Who was the main advocate for the distribution of DC electricity to cities?
Edison
Faraday
Tesla
Westinghouse
Think of the 'war of the currents': which of the two rival electrical systems was adopted for city supply, and who pushed each one?
Only one of the four names is associated with building a system for distributing electricity to homes and streets.
A
Thomas Edison developed and promoted a DC system (about 110 V with a network of substations) and was the main advocate for distributing DC electricity to cities.

Westinghouse adopted Tesla's AC system, which could be transformed to higher voltages for transmission and so became standard for long-distance supply. Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction but was not involved in urban distribution, and Tesla is associated with AC rather than DC.

content.text: Which of the following is an inertial frame of reference?
A rocket during launch
A train travelling at a constant velocity
A car turning a corner at a constant speed
A lift slowing down as it approaches the ground floor
An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds: an object at rest, or moving at constant velocity, needs no net force to keep doing what it is doing.
Test each case for acceleration, including the change in direction of a constant-speed turn, and remember that accelerating frames feel a fictitious force.
B

In an inertial frame the net force on an object is zero whenever its velocity is constant. A train travelling at a constant velocity in a straight line satisfies this, so it is an inertial frame of reference.

The others are all accelerating: a rocket during launch, a car turning a corner at constant speed (its direction of velocity is changing, so it has a centripetal acceleration) and a lift slowing down. Accelerating frames are non-inertial because objects appear to accelerate when no real force acts on them.

Two horizontal parallel charged plates, the upper marked with three minus signs and the lower with three plus signs. Three parallel field lines with arrowheads point from the negative upper plate downward to the positive lower plate, i.e. against the electric field direction.

Two horizontal parallel charged plates, the upper marked with three minus signs and the lower with three plus signs. Three horizontal field lines with arrowheads all point to the right, so the field runs parallel to the plates instead of across the gap.

content.text: Field lines start on positive charge, finish on negative charge, and between large parallel plates they are straight, parallel and equally spaced.
Check two things in each diagram: whether the arrowheads run from the $+$ plate to the $-$ plate, and whether the lines cross the gap or run along the plates.
A
The field of parallel plates is uniform: the lines run straight across the gap, perpendicular to the plates, and point from the positive plate towards the negative plate.
The diagram showing straight, parallel, equally spaced lines with arrowheads pointing from the lower positive plate up to the upper negative plate is therefore the correct one.

The diagrams with lines running parallel to the plates are impossible, since a field component along the plates would not be produced by the surface charge on them, and the diagram with the arrows reversed (from the $-$ plate to the $+$ plate) has the field direction backwards.

content.text: An electric current flows in undoped silicon. Which statement about this current is true?
The number of electrons moving exceeds the number of holes moving.
The number of holes moving exceeds the number of electrons moving.
Equal numbers of holes and electrons are moving in the same direction.
Equal numbers of holes and electrons are moving in opposite directions.
In intrinsic (undoped) silicon every free electron in the conduction band leaves a hole behind in the valence band, so the two populations are equal.
Then apply $F = qE$ to each carrier and remember that a hole behaves as a positive charge, so it drifts along the field while the electron drifts against it.
D

Undoped silicon is an intrinsic semiconductor: each conduction electron is paired with one valence-band hole, so equal numbers of electrons and holes carry the current. This rules out the options claiming more electrons than holes or more holes than electrons.

In the applied field the negatively charged electrons drift against the field while the positively charged holes drift along it, so the two carriers move in opposite directions. Their contributions to the current add rather than cancel, which is why intrinsic silicon conducts.

content.text: Which of the following best represents the structure of a metallic lattice?

content.alt_text: A regular square array of circled plus signs (positive metal ions) with circled minus signs (conduction electrons) spaced midway between them in an orderly repeating lattice.

content.text: A metal is a regular lattice of positive metal ions with a 'sea' of delocalised electrons spread throughout the structure - the electrons are not attached to particular ions.
Look for the diagram with an ordered array of positive ions AND electrons distributed freely between them, rather than electrons fixed to sites, tied to ions, or gathered into a separate layer.
B

In a metal the positive metal ions occupy fixed positions in a regular repeating lattice, and the valence electrons are delocalised: they are free to move anywhere within the structure instead of being bound to particular ions. This 'sea of electrons' model leaves the metal overall neutral and explains its conductivity.
The correct diagram therefore shows the positive ions in an ordered lattice with the electrons scattered randomly through the spaces between them, which is the diagram keyed here.

The diagram with electrons locked into fixed, ordered sites between the ions shows localised electrons, which could not conduct. The diagram pairing each electron with particular ions, and the diagram with all the electrons in a separate layer away from the ions, describe structures that are not metallic lattices.

content.text: Which of the following is a correct statement about the Michelson–Morley experiment?
It proved the existence of the luminiferous aether.
It compared the speeds of light rays travelling along parallel paths.
It was invalid because the equipment was not sufficiently sensitive.
It was unable to detect the motion of Earth through the luminiferous aether.
What did the null result actually show, and what can and cannot be concluded from a null result?
Consider the geometry of the two light paths in the interferometer and whether a failure to detect an effect means the experiment was faulty.
D

Michelson and Morley compared the round-trip travel times of two light rays travelling along perpendicular arms of an interferometer as the apparatus was rotated, looking for a fringe shift caused by an 'aether wind' from Earth's motion. They detected none, so they were unable to detect the motion of Earth through the luminiferous aether.

It did not prove the aether existed; that is the opposite of what a null result shows. The two beams travelled along perpendicular, not parallel, paths. Nor was the experiment invalid because of poor sensitivity: it was a careful, repeatable test whose null result was later explained by special relativity, in which there is no aether to detect.

content.text: An electron is fired in a vacuum towards a screen. With no electric field being applied, the electron hits the screen at $P$. A uniform electric field is turned on and another electron is fired towards the screen from the same location, at the same velocity, striking the screen at point $Q$.

content.alt_text: A grey rectangular screen. A row of four labelled open circles A, B, C and D runs across it from left to right. Two filled star markers sit on the screen between A and B (labelled Q below) and between B and C (labelled P below), showing the undeviated strike point P and the deflected strike point Q. The word Screen sits above with a leader line into the rectangle.

content.text: With the electric field still turned on, a proton is fired towards the screen from the same starting point as the electrons and with the same velocity.
At what point does the proton strike the screen?
A
B
C
D
Use the displacement of the electron from P to Q to work out which way the uniform field points: $F = qE$ and the electron is negatively charged.
Then compare the force on the proton with that on the electron - same size of charge, same speed, same field, but opposite sign of charge.
C

With no field the electron strikes at P; with the field on it strikes at Q, which lies to the left of P (between A and B). The force on the electron is therefore to the left, and since $F = qE$ with $q$ negative the field must point to the right.

The proton carries the same magnitude of charge and is fired at the same velocity through the same field, so $|F| = |q|E$ is the same size. Because the proton is positively charged, its force is to the right, i.e. the mirror image of the electron's deflection.

The proton is therefore deflected by the same distance to the other side of P. Since P lies between B and C, the point the same distance beyond P on the other side lies between C and D, i.e. the proton strikes at C.

content.text: What does the Maltese cross apparatus demonstrate about cathode rays?
They travel in straight lines.
They consist of a beam of electrons.
They are absorbed by a metal surface.
They are not affected by magnetic fields.
The cross casts a shadow on the screen. What must the rays be doing for a shadow of that exact shape to appear?
Be careful about what a shadow can and cannot tell you: it shows direction of travel, not the identity of the particles or their absorption by all surfaces.
A

The Maltese cross casts a clear shadow of its own shape on the screen, with a sharp edge. That is only possible if the cathode rays travel in straight lines from the cathode, through the cross, to the screen - if they bent around the cross, no sharp shadow would form.

That the rays are a beam of electrons was established by other experiments, such as their deflection by electric and magnetic fields. The shadow does not show that the rays are absorbed by a metal surface (the cross is a thin obstruction, not a closed metal screen), and cathode rays are in fact deflected by magnetic fields.

content.text: The diagram shows a model of a generator connected to a galvanometer.

content.alt_text: A model generator between the poles of two magnets, N on the left and S on the right. A rectangular coil rotates about a central horizontal axis drawn as a dashed line; arrows on both sides of the coil are labelled Rotation and curve downwards on the right. content.text: The loop is rotated continuously in a clockwise direction as viewed from the end nearest the galvanometer.
Which row of the table correctly identifies the type of generator and the movement of the needle of the galvanometer?
DC generator; the needle swings between 0 and $+$.
AC generator; the needle swings between $-$ and 0.
DC generator; the needle swings between $+$ and $-$.
AC generator; the needle swings between $-$ and $+$.
Look closely at the rings on the shaft: are they continuous slip rings or is each one divided into two halves?
Then ask what happens to the coil current over one revolution, and what the galvanometer therefore reads as the connection to the coil is swapped twice per turn.
A

Each ring on the shaft is divided into two halves and the brushes contact the two halves, so this is a split-ring commutator, not a pair of slip rings. The connection to the external circuit is therefore reversed every half turn, the alternating emf in the rotating coil is rectified, and the generator produces DC.

The induced emf in the coil reverses direction each half revolution, but the commutator changes which half-ring each brush touches at exactly those instants, so the current through the galvanometer always flows the same way round the external circuit.

Applying the right-hand rule to the coil rotating clockwise as viewed from the galvanometer end, with the N pole on the left and the S pole on the right, shows that the current always enters the positive terminal of the galvanometer. The needle therefore deflects to one side and returns to zero twice each revolution: it swings between 0 and $+$. The AC rows are wrong because the rings are split, and the row with the needle swinging through both sides of zero is wrong because the current never reverses in the external circuit.

content.text: Which row of the table correctly identifies the position at which the satellite has greater kinetic energy and the position at which it has greater potential energy?
Greater kinetic energy at $X$; greater potential energy at $X$.
Greater kinetic energy at $X$; greater potential energy at $Y$.
Greater kinetic energy at $Y$; greater potential energy at $X$.
Greater kinetic energy at $Y$; greater potential energy at $Y$.

In an orbit the total mechanical energy is constant, so kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy must vary in opposite ways: as the satellite moves closer to Earth its potential energy becomes more negative and its kinetic energy rises.
Decide separately which labelled point is the near point of the orbit and which is the far point, then match each energy to the position at which it is larger.
B

Gravitational potential energy is $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so it is largest (least negative) at the point of the orbit furthest from Earth. Kinetic and potential energy trade over the orbit, so the satellite is fastest and has the greatest kinetic energy at the point closest to Earth, where the potential energy is smallest. $X$ is the near point and $Y$ is the far point, so the greater kinetic energy is at $X$ and the greater potential energy at $Y$: the second row, option B.

The rows that place both energies at the same position are impossible because both energies change continuously around an elliptical orbit, and the row with $Y$ for the kinetic energy has the two swapped.

content.text: A triangular piece of wire is placed in a magnetic field as shown.

content.alt_text: A triangular piece of wire PQR sits in a uniform magnetic field drawn as seven horizontal lines with arrowheads pointing to the right. A battery symbol sits on side PQ. Current $I$ flows along PR from P to R. A dashed vertical line through Q is the axis WX, and a dashed horizontal line through the middle of the triangle is the axis YZ.

content.text: When current $I$ is supplied as shown, how does the wire move?
Axis of rotation $YZ$; $Q$ moves into the page.
Axis of rotation $YZ$; $Q$ moves out of the page.
Axis of rotation $WX$; $R$ moves into the page.
Axis of rotation $WX$; $R$ moves out of the page.
Work out the magnetic force on each side of the triangle separately using $F = BIl\sin\theta$, remembering that a section carrying current parallel to the field lines feels no force at all.

The resulting force is at right angles to the plane of the triangle, so the two non-zero forces act as a couple. Ask which axis of rotation that couple is about, and which corner is pushed into the page.
C

The base $PR$ carries current parallel to the field lines, so $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ and the force on it is zero. The current in the left side $PQ$ runs from $Q$ down to $P$, and the right-hand rule for $I\mathbf{l}\times\mathbf{B}$ gives a force out of the page. On the right side $QR$ the current runs from $R$ up to $Q$ and the force is into the page.

These two forces are equal and opposite and act on opposite sides of the triangle, so the net force is zero and they form a couple. The couple turns the triangle about the vertical dashed axis $WX$, the only axis marked that lies in the plane of the triangle and is perpendicular to both forces. The point $R$ lies on the side whose force is directed into the page, so $R$ moves into the page. That is option C; the rows using axis $YZ$ would require a force component lying inside the plane of the triangle, which the geometry does not produce.

content.text: The potential differences $V_1$ and $V_2$ are measured continuously for $4\,\mathrm{s}$. The switch is initially closed.
At $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, the switch is opened.
Which pair of graphs shows how the potential differences $V_1$ and $V_2$ vary with time over the 4-second interval?

content.alt_text: A pair of graphs. V1 starts at a constant positive value, drops to zero at t = 2 s and stays at zero to t = 4 s. V2 is zero except for a single narrow positive spike at t = 2 s. Both horizontal axes are Time (s) marked 0 to 4.

A pair of graphs. V1 starts at a constant positive value, drops to zero at t = 2 s and stays at zero to t = 4 s. V2 is a full sinusoid swinging positive then negative between t = 0 and t = 4 s. Both horizontal axes are Time (s) marked 0 to 4.

A pair of graphs. V1 is zero until t = 2 s then steps up to a constant positive value to t = 4 s. V2 is zero except for a single narrow negative spike at t = 2 s. Both horizontal axes are Time (s) marked 0 to 4.

content.text: A steady direct current produces a constant magnetic flux in the core, and the secondary emf depends on the rate of change of that flux, not on the flux itself.
Track $V_1$ first: it is the potential difference across a resistor in the primary loop, so it can only be non-zero while a current flows.
Then look for the single instant at which the primary flux changes abruptly, because that is the only moment the secondary can respond.
A

With the switch closed a steady direct current flows in the primary loop, so the flux in the core is constant, $\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = 0$, and no emf is induced in the secondary: $V_2 = 0$. The current through the primary resistor, and hence $V_1$, is constant and positive for $0 < t < 2\,\mathrm{s}$.

When the switch is opened at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$ the primary current collapses, so $V_1$ falls to zero and stays there. That collapse is itself a rapid change of flux in the core, and it induces a single narrow pulse in the secondary at exactly $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, after which $V_2$ returns to zero. Only the first pair of graphs shows a constant $V_1$ that falls to zero at $2\,\mathrm{s}$ together with one narrow pulse on $V_2$: option A. Option B wrongly shows a continuous alternating $V_2$, which a DC input cannot produce, and options C and D wrongly show $V_1$ rising only after the switch has been opened.

An acceleration–time graph over 20 s. The trace is zero, steps up to a small constant positive value, then steps up again to a larger constant positive value before dropping back to zero near the end of the interval.

content.text: Look carefully at the orientation of the $X$–$X'$ axis on the car: it runs across the car from side to side, so the accelerometer responds to sideways acceleration, not to changes in the car's speed.
On the circular part of the path the sideways acceleration has constant magnitude $v^2/r$ and always acts towards the same side of the car; on the straight approach and departure roads it is zero.
The car has to swing the other way as it joins the roundabout and again as it leaves it, so check the sign of the trace at those two short transitions as well as along the middle.
B

Because the $X$–$X'$ axis is mounted across the car, the accelerometer measures the component of acceleration perpendicular to the direction of travel. On the straight roads either side of the roundabout the acceleration is zero, so the trace is zero at the start and at the end. Entering the roundabout the car swings to the left, so the reading is briefly negative. On the circular part the acceleration is centripetal, of constant magnitude $v^2/r$ because the speed and radius are both constant, and for a turn in one sense it always acts towards the inside of the turn, which stays on the same side of the car: a constant positive plateau. Leaving the roundabout the car swings left again, giving a second brief negative pulse.

That trace — zero, short negative pulse, constant positive plateau, short negative pulse, zero — is option B. Option A is wrong because it shows the reading at zero for most of the journey; option C has the entry and exit pulses the same sign as the plateau, which would mean the car never turned the other way; option D has no pulses at all and so ignores the approach and departure curves.

content.text: At what point during the rotation of the wire does the maximum current flow in a direction from $P$ to $Q$ through the moving part of the wire?

Read the first diagram carefully: it is a vertical cross-section with north at the top, so the field at the equator is horizontal and points north, while the line $XY$ on which the two students stand runs east–west. The field is therefore across the wire, not along it.

The loop is turned about the horizontal axis $PQ$, so the angle between the field and the loop's normal keeps changing. The induced emf is greatest when the flux is changing fastest, which is when the flux through the loop is zero.
Use Lenz's law to fix the sense of the induced current, then match that sense to the labelled points on the turning wire.
C

The field-line diagram is a vertical cross-section of the Earth with north at the top of the page. At the equator the field is horizontal and directed north, which on that diagram means it crosses the equator upwards; the line $XY$ along which the two students stand lies along the equatorial east–west direction. The field is therefore perpendicular to the wire $PQ$.

As the loop is turned about the horizontal axis $PQ$, the flux linking it swings between $+BA$, when the loop stands upright with its normal parallel to the field, and zero, when the loop is turned edge-on. The induced emf, $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$, is greatest where the flux is changing fastest, and that is where the flux passes through zero: the instant at which the turning wire is seen edge-on as the narrow vertical dashed segment, where the wire at $A$ is on the upward stroke and the wire at $C$ is on the downward stroke.

Lenz's law fixes the sense of the induced current. As the flux through the loop falls, the induced current flows so as to sustain it, and on the pass of the rotation in which the wire at $C$ is sweeping downwards that current runs from $P$ to $Q$ through the moving section. Its magnitude is greatest at that edge-on instant, so the maximum current in the $P$ to $Q$ direction occurs at $C$.

content.text: Contrast the design of transformers and magnetic braking systems in terms of the effects that eddy currents have in these devices.
Both devices rely on electromagnetic induction, so ask the same two questions of each: is a changing flux wanted here, and is the energy lost as heat wanted here?

For a transformer, ask whether the current induced in the iron core is wanted. If it is not, then the core's construction has to be designed to limit it, and the limiting principle is the same one that governs the size of an induced current.

For a magnetic brake the induced current is the whole point of the device, so the design must do the opposite: maximise the current, and think about what large current path does to the energy of the moving object.

Transformers are laminated to minimise eddy currents and the resistive heating they cause, while magnetic braking systems use large solid sheets of copper to maximise eddy currents so that kinetic energy is converted to heat.

A transformer uses changes in magnetic flux to induce a current in a secondary coil. An iron core increases the flux but iron, being a conductor, will experience the induction of unwanted eddy currents, causing resistive heating losses. Laminating the iron core minimises the current pathway, thus minimising eddy currents and the subsequent heating losses. In contrast, magnetic braking systems need to maximise eddy currents, since magnetic braking relies on converting kinetic energy to electrical current and subsequently to heat. In order to maximise the current, magnetic braking systems need to provide a substantial current pathway, which is done by providing large sheets or bulk volumes of conductive material such as copper.

items: (a)(i) Wegener's notion of drifting continents went against existing dogma, and his explanations were inadequate in accounting for the scale of the movement of the continents; alternative explanations could be provided for the observations, so there was no pressure to change.

(a)(ii) Analysis of magnetic reversals in the crustal rocks showed a symmetry on either side of mid-ocean ridges that was consistent with sea-floor spreading, and the age of the rocks increased with distance from the mid-ocean ridges. Both are consistent with sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics. (A relationship between magnetism and polar wandering is also acceptable.)

content.text: (a)(i) Two reasons: the theory contradicted established dogma about the permanence of the continents, and the proposed mechanism could not account for the scale of the movement. Because competing explanations existed for the fossil and rock observations, there was no compelling reason to accept the new idea.

(a)(ii) As basaltic lava solidifies at a ridge it cools below the Curie temperature, and iron-bearing minerals align with Earth's current magnetic field and then lock that direction in. When Earth's field later reverses, newly formed crust records the opposite direction. Walking away from the ridge you therefore meet a symmetric, repeating sequence of normal and reversed bands.

The increasing age of the rock with distance from the ridge shows that crust is being created continuously at the ridge and carried away from it, and the mirrored reversal sequence shows that both sides of the ridge are being created at the same time. Neither observation is possible on a static Earth, so together they are direct physical evidence for sea-floor spreading and hence for plate tectonics.

content.text: Seismic waves and the solid–liquid boundary
Sub-part (b)(i) is about particle motion, not wave motion: compare the direction in which each wave vibrates its particles with the direction in which the energy travels.

For (b)(ii) decide first which of the two waves can survive in a liquid, then say what both waves do when they reach the boundary at all. Remember that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items: (b)(i) The particles transferring energy in the form of a $P$ wave oscillate parallel to the direction of energy propagation, whereas the particles transferring energy in the form of an $S$ wave oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation.

(b)(ii) Both $P$ and $S$ waves are reflected at the boundary at the same angle as the angle of incidence. Only the $P$ wave crosses the boundary and travels into the liquid, because a liquid cannot support a shear stress. The $P$ wave is refracted as it crosses the solid–liquid boundary, since its speed changes on entering the liquid.

content.text: (b)(i) A $P$ wave is a compression (longitudinal) wave: the oscillation of the particles is along the line in which the wave energy travels. An $S$ wave is a shear (transverse) wave: the particles oscillate across, at right angles to the direction in which the wave energy travels. Both can pass through the same solid because a solid can support both compressional and shear stresses.
(b)(ii) The ray in the diagram strikes a solid–liquid boundary from above. At that boundary the wave is partly reflected back into the solid and partly transmitted.

Shear stress cannot be transmitted by a liquid, so no $S$ wave passes into the liquid and the $S$ wave is completely reflected. The $P$ wave is partly transmitted, but its speed changes on entering the liquid, so the transmitted ray is refracted and its path changes direction. Reflection and refraction are separate effects: the reflection angle depends only on the angle of incidence, while the refraction depends on the change in wave speed.

content.text: Describe TWO different methods that can be used to calculate the mass of Earth. In your answer, refer to the relevant equations.
Each method must be paired with the equation you would actually rearrange, and every quantity in that equation must be something you can measure without already knowing the mass of Earth.

Either combine $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$ with a measured $g$ and $r$, or apply Kepler's law to a satellite orbit using $r^{3} = \dfrac{GM T^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}$.

One method to calculate the mass of Earth is to use the relationship between the strength of the gravitational field and the radius of Earth and its mass. Gravitational field strength and the radius of Earth can be experimentally determined: $F = mg = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}$ gives $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$, hence $M = \dfrac{gr^{2}}{G}$. Another method is to apply Kepler's law using data from a satellite's orbit; both the radius and the period of a satellite can be experimentally determined, and $\dfrac{4\pi^{2} r^{3}}{T^{2}} = GM$ gives $M = \dfrac{4\pi^{2} r^{3}}{GT^{2}}$. Answers could also include the pendulum method.

content.text: Gravimeters and gravity survey data reduction

Sub-part (d)(i) is about the instrument: name the physical principle the design relies on, then say how that principle is turned into a readable value of $g$. Sub-part (d)(ii) is about correcting readings, so list the separate effects of the two locations on the reading before you justify anything.

items: (d)(i) One type of gravimeter uses the inertial properties of a mass confined by springs in a vacuum. The effect of gravity on the confined mass causes it to move independently of the surrounding housing, and this movement is calibrated against variations in the strength of gravity so that the instrument can be used to directly measure the strength of gravity.

(d)(ii) Data reduction removes the effects on the measurement of gravity that are caused by features associated with specific locations, which allows valid comparisons between the locations independent of those features. The effect on gravimeter readings of the rotation of Earth on its axis is greater at the Equator ($X$) than at higher latitudes ($Y$), reducing the readings more at the Equator. At the higher altitude of $Y$ the reduction in the gravimeter readings is greater than at the lower altitude of $X$.

content.text: (d)(i) In the common spring gravimeter a mass is suspended by springs inside a vacuum housing. Acceleration due to gravity moves the mass independently of the housing; the small displacement of the mass relative to the housing is amplified and calibrated so that the instrument displays the value of $g$. An absolute gravimeter instead measures the free-fall acceleration of test masses levitated in vacuum. Either design earns the marks.

(d)(ii) A gravimeter measures the local value of $g$, but $g$ is not constant across the globe, so raw readings cannot be compared directly. Two features of the locations in the diagram change the reading:

items: Earth's rotation: the equatorial region moves fastest, so the centrifugal effect reduces the measured value of $g$ more at the Equator ($X$) than at the higher latitude ($Y$).

Altitude: since $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$, being further from Earth's centre reduces the reading. Site $Y$ is a 5000 m mountain and site $X$ a 200 m mountain, so $Y$ is higher above the centre of Earth and reads lower.

content.text: Data reduction subtracts these known corrections from the raw readings. Only then can readings from different sites be compared to reveal the density variations of the underlying rock, which is the actual objective of a gravity survey.

content.text: Endoscopes: fibre bundles and image formation
Sub-part (a)(i) turns on a single question: does each fibre leave the bundle at the same place it entered? Sub-part (a)(ii) needs the mechanism that keeps light inside a fibre.
For (a)(ii) remember that an endoscope carries light in and an image out through two separate bundles. Ask what each bundle is for, and which one has to preserve the spatial arrangement of the light.

items: (a)(i) In a coherent bundle the relative position of the individual fibres is the same at each end. In an incoherent bundle the relative position is not maintained.

(a)(ii) Endoscopy relies on the physical principle of total internal reflection: light is reflected within each fibre and thereby manipulated. The incoherent bundles provide illumination to the site, which would otherwise be in darkness. This then permits the coherent bundles to transmit an image to a camera for external viewing.

content.text: (a)(i) A fibre bundle is made of thousands of thin optical fibres. If every fibre occupies the same relative position at both ends, the bundle is coherent and the spatial pattern of light at the far end is transferred faithfully to the near end. In an incoherent bundle the fibres are randomly ordered, so the pattern is scrambled and only an average illumination can be transmitted.

(a)(ii) Each fibre has a core of higher refractive index surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light striking the core–cladding boundary above the critical angle is totally internally reflected, so light travels along the fibre by a series of internal reflections even around tight bends.

The endoscope therefore contains two bundles. The incoherent bundle carries lamp light to the tip purely to illuminate the internal surface, which would otherwise be in darkness. The coherent bundle then carries light reflected from that surface and preserves its spatial arrangement, so the eye of the endoscope forms a real, upright image of the organ wall which a camera records for external viewing.

content.text: Ultrasound imaging
Sub-part (b)(i) asks for a measurement method: say what is aimed at the bone, what is detected afterwards, and how the detected quantity relates to the bone property.

For (b)(ii) think about what happens to penetration and to resolution when the frequency changes. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, which means both greater detail and less penetration, and the two scan types need one of each.

items: (b)(i) Measurement of bone density can be made by directing ultrasound waves at a bone (eg the heel bone) and measuring the amount of waves transmitted. The higher the bone density, the more ultrasound waves are absorbed and therefore fewer are transmitted.

(b)(ii) $B$ scans are used to examine eyes and therefore have no need to penetrate tissue more than a few centimetres, so a higher frequency ($20\,\mathrm{MHz}$) can be used to obtain greater detail. Sector scans are used to examine tissues deep within the body, eg a pregnant uterus. By using a lower frequency ($3.5\,\mathrm{MHz}$), a greater depth of tissue can be examined, albeit with less detail.

content.text: (b)(i) Ultrasound is partially absorbed as it passes through tissue, and the amount absorbed depends on the density of the material. Directing a pulse at a bone and comparing the intensity that gets through with the intensity sent in gives a measure of how much the bone absorbs, which is related to its density. This is the basis of clinical bone-density measurement.

(b)(ii) The frequency fixes the wavelength through $v = f\lambda$, and the wavelength fixes both the resolution (the smallest detail that can be distinguished) and the amount of scattering and absorption in tissue.

A $B$ scan images a structure only a few centimetres away, such as the eye. Its short wavelength gives good resolution, which is why the highest frequency is used and the shallow penetration is not a problem.

A sector scan images deep organs such as a pregnant uterus, where the beam must survive tens of centimetres of tissue. A longer wavelength is scattered and absorbed less, so the pulse reaches the deep tissue and returns. The price is a coarser image, since resolution scales with wavelength.

content.text: Explain how the application of a radio frequency wave changes the behaviour of nuclei with net spin in a strong, external magnetic field.

Start by describing what the nuclei are doing in $B_{0}$ before any radio frequency is applied: the two possible orientations, which of them is lower in energy, and the direction in which the nuclei precess.

Then ask what happens when a radio frequency wave is tuned to that precession rate. Only nuclei already precessing at that rate can absorb the energy, so what does absorption do to their energy level and to the phase relationship between them?
A radio frequency wave at the Larmor frequency is absorbed by the lower-energy spin-up nuclei, flipping them to the higher-energy spin-down orientation so that they precess in phase.

Nuclei with net spin line up with the external magnetic field, $B_0$. Their orientation may be in one of two ways — lower energy spin up or higher energy spin down — with slightly more in the lower energy state. At the same time, these nuclei precess around the direction of $B_0$ with a frequency (Larmor frequency) that is dependent on the magnitude of $B_0$, the type of nucleus and its immediate environment. When a radio frequency corresponding to the Larmor frequency is applied, the lower energy spin up nuclei absorb the energy and flip to spin down orientation, then precess in phase with each other. Nuclei which precess at different frequencies are unaffected.

content.text: X-ray and CAT imaging

Sub-part (d)(i) is a production chain: something is accelerated, it strikes a target, and the deceleration produces the radiation. Sub-part (d)(ii) is about what a plain X-ray film records versus what a computed scan reconstructs.
For (d)(ii) ask what a single point on a plain X-ray image actually represents. If it stands for several centimetres of tissue all at once, that is the source of the ambiguity.

items: (d)(i) Electrons are accelerated to high velocities by a high voltage. When they strike the tungsten target, their rapid deceleration produces electromagnetic radiation in the X-ray range of the spectrum.

(d)(ii) X-ray images are formed by the shadows cast on a film (or digital detector) in which each point on the image represents all of the tissue in front of it, often several centimetres in depth. A CAT scan uses tomography to gather information on X-ray attenuation that can be organised into slices. This provides a clearer image as there is no superimposition of other layers.

content.text: (d)(i) In the tube, electrons are released by thermal emission and accelerated through a high potential difference. They strike the tungsten anode and decelerate sharply, radiating electromagnetic energy; only a small fraction of their kinetic energy is converted into X-ray photons, the rest becoming heat.

(d)(ii) In a conventional radiograph a wide beam passes through the body in one direction and the detector integrates everything in front of it, so the image is a projection of all the intervening tissue. Overlapping structures cannot be separated, and structures of similar attenuation cannot be told apart.

A CAT scanner instead uses a narrow beam and a co-rotating detector to collect X-ray attenuation data from many angles around the body. A computer reconstructs these measurements into cross-sectional slices, and any plane can be assembled from them. Because each point of the image now corresponds to one small volume of tissue rather than a whole column, the image is clearer, is unambiguous, and gives better soft-tissue differentiation, at a higher cost and a larger radiation dose.

PET and gamma-emitting bone scans image the uptake of injected radioisotopes, which depends on how the body is working, so abnormal processes invisible to structural scans can be detected earlier and treated more effectively.

PET scans and bone scans using gamma radiation are two functional imaging techniques. In both of these the uptake of radioisotopes used to produce the images is dependent on how the body is working. items: (b)(i) The spectrum of star $X$ (hot, spectral type B) shows the highest intensity in the blue, short-wavelength part of the spectrum, with ionised helium lines and a strong ultraviolet component. The spectrum of star $Y$ (cool, spectral type M) shows the highest intensity in the red, long-wavelength part of the spectrum, with dominant molecular lines and strong neutral metal lines.

content.text: Composition of the He-3 nucleus and the strong nuclear force
Sub-part (a)(i) is a bookkeeping exercise: use the mass number and the atomic number to work out how many protons and how many neutrons, then remember that each of those is built from three quarks.

Sub-part (a)(ii) needs the shape of the strong force, not just its size. Think about what happens to its strength as nucleons approach each other and then move apart, and compare it with the electrostatic force between protons.

items: (a)(i) The helium-3 nucleus consists of 1 neutron and 2 protons (3 nucleons), which are themselves made up of three quarks each — 9 quarks in total.

(a)(ii) The strong nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion and acts over only very small distances. It is extremely attractive between nucleons about 1 fm apart, decreases rapidly at distances greater than about 2.5 fm, and becomes repulsive at distances less than about 0.7 fm.

content.text: (a)(i) He-3 has mass number 3 and atomic number 2. The two protons account for a mass number of 2, leaving $3 - 2 = 1$ neutron. Each proton is a uud and each neutron is a udd, so the nucleus contains $2 \times 3 + 1 \times 3 = 9$ quarks.

(a)(ii) The strong nuclear force is one of the four fundamental forces and is by far the strongest of them, but its range is only a few femtometres. Within that range it dominates the Coulomb repulsion between the protons in the nucleus, which is what holds the nucleus together.

items: At separations of about 1 fm it is extremely attractive, binding the nucleons together.
Beyond about 2.5 fm it falls off rapidly, so it cannot hold distant parts of a large nucleus together — which is why very heavy nuclei are unstable.
Below about 0.7 fm it becomes repulsive, which prevents all the nucleons collapsing to a single point and sets the nuclear density.

content.text: Fission, transmutation and reactor components

Sub-part (b)(i) is a distinguish-between question, so you need a comparison that separates the two processes, not two separate definitions. Sub-part (b)(ii) asks about three labelled components; give each one its own job.
For (b)(ii) follow the neutron: where does it come from, what must happen to it before it can cause another fission, and what stops too many of them happening?

items: (b)(i) A transmutation involves an atomic nucleus turning into that of another element, by radioactive decay or by nuclear bombardment. Fission involves the splitting of an atom into smaller, similar-sized fragments due to the capturing of a neutron, and this process releases energy.

(b)(ii) Fuel elements are a fissile material that releases energy and high-speed neutrons when atoms are split. The moderator slows the neutrons down so that they can be captured by more fissile atoms, which then split. The control rods absorb neutrons to limit the number of atoms undergoing fission, thereby controlling the release of energy.

content.text: (b)(i) The distinguishing features are what causes the change and what the change produces. Transmutation changes the identity of the element, producing a different nucleus, and may be triggered by random decay or by deliberate bombardment; it does not necessarily release useful energy. Fission splits one heavy nucleus into two roughly similar lighter nuclei plus neutrons, and the mass defect of the split appears as released energy.
(b)(ii) Each labelled component has a separate role in the chain reaction:

items: Fuel element: a fissile material. When it captures a slow neutron its nucleus becomes unstable and fissions, releasing energy and two or three further fast neutrons.

Moderator: slows the fast neutrons down to thermal energies, where their chance of being captured by a further fissile nucleus is high. Each capture releases more neutrons, sustaining the chain reaction at a steady rate.

Control rods: made of a material such as boron or cadmium that absorbs neutrons. Pushing the rods further into the core absorbs more neutrons, fewer atoms split, and the reaction slows; withdrawing them lets more neutrons cause fission and the rate of energy release rises.

content.text: It is the combination of the three that gives a controlled reaction: the fuel supplies both the energy and the neutrons, the moderator keeps the neutron population in the range where fission is likely, and the control rods set and adjust the overall rate.

content.text: With reference to Bohr's postulates, explain how the line at 434.0 nm in the hydrogen emission spectrum is produced. Support your answer with calculations.

Identify which series the line belongs to before doing any arithmetic — 434.0 nm is visible light, so look on the diagram for the series whose lines terminate at a level and fall in the visible range.

Bohr's postulates give you the physics and the Rydberg equation gives you the number. Decide whether you want to solve for the initial level or for the wavelength, and write the substitution with the wavelength converted to metres.
An electron drops from $n = 5$ to $n = 2$ (Balmer series), emitting a photon of wavelength 434.0 nm.

Bohr's postulates state that an electron orbits in fixed energy levels. Only when an electron jumps from a higher energy level to a lower energy level does it emit an exact amount of energy in the form of a photon. The specific wavelength of the photon can be determined according to the Rydberg equation. The blue light is part of the visible Balmer series and therefore $n_f = 2$. The wavelength in this case is 434.0 nm. According to the equation, this corresponds to a jump from the 5th energy level to the 2nd energy level. For the Balmer series $n_f = 2$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right) = 1.097\times 10^{7} \left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$. Substituting $\lambda = 434\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$ gives $n_i = 5$. Answers could also substitute $n_i = 5$ and $n_f = 2$ to obtain $\lambda = 434.0\,\mathrm{nm}$.

content.text: Limitations of the Bohr model
Sub-part (d)(i) is a conflict between two things: what the Bohr model needs (stable orbits) and what classical physics predicts for an accelerating charge. Write the two predictions side by side.
For (d)(ii) the fix is a new model of the electron — treat it as a wave rather than a particle on a track — and then name the experiment that tested the new model.

items: (d)(i) The stable electron orbits necessary for the Bohr model assumed that the electron was travelling in circular motion about the nucleus. This would mean that the electron is constantly accelerating. But since accelerating charges give out electromagnetic radiation, the electron would lose energy and spiral in towards the nucleus.

(d)(ii) de Broglie modelled the electrons as existing as standing waves about the nucleus, with each of Bohr's stationary states (energy levels) associated with various wavelengths, so that only integer multiples of the fundamental wavelength were possible. Davisson and Germer then validated this model with their electron-scattering experiment, which provided evidence that electrons were waves.

content.text: (d)(i) Bohr postulated that electrons occupy certain fixed orbits and do not radiate. Classical electrodynamics says that any charge undergoing centripetal (circular) acceleration continuously emits electromagnetic radiation and therefore loses energy. The orbital energy would decrease, the electron would move in an ever-smaller orbit, and within about $10^{-11}\,\mathrm{s}$ it would collapse into the nucleus. The two predictions are incompatible, so the stable orbits cannot be derived from classical physics.

(d)(ii) de Broglie proposed that the electron in each allowed orbit behaves as a standing wave about the nucleus. The circumference of an orbit must then contain a whole number of half-wavelengths, which quantises the possible orbits.

Davisson and Germer fired electrons at a nickel crystal and observed a diffraction pattern in the scattered electrons. The angles matched those predicted for wave diffraction, confirming the de Broglie wavelength and so validating the standing-wave model of the atom.

content.text: Explain how the properties of protons and neutrons contribute to their uses as tools for investigating matter.
Write a separate paragraph for the proton and a separate one for the neutron; do not mix their properties. In each paragraph, end by naming the use that the property makes possible.

The top band needs the link to be explicit for both particles: charge for the proton (accelerate it, collide it, convert energy into mass), and no charge plus wave nature for the neutron (get close to nuclei, diffract).

The proton's positive charge lets it be accelerated to high energies and used in collisions to create and detect new particles; the neutral neutron can approach nuclei closely and its very small de Broglie wavelength gives diffraction patterns that reveal atomic and molecular structure.

Protons and neutrons have almost identical masses but the proton is positively charged and the neutron has no charge. Having a positive charge allows protons to be accelerated to very high velocities in particle accelerators. The protons then collide head-on with other protons, transferring their energy to mass ($E = mc^{2}$) and producing other particles which can be detected through their interaction with large detectors. This allows us to discover new particles and study the fundamental nature of matter. In studying normal matter, protons cannot get close enough since they are repelled by the positive nucleus. Instead, neutron beams can be fired at nuclei in a process known as neutron scattering. Since all matter has a dual particle/wave nature, neutrons, having a very small de Broglie wavelength, can produce diffraction patterns giving us detailed models of atomic and molecular structures.

content.text: Logic gates and data storage
Read the gate symbol carefully: the extra curved line on the input side is what identifies it. Then work through the truth table row by row.
For (a)(ii) treat the two gates as a pair. First work out what gate H must output given that its inputs are $R$ and $Q$, then feed that into gate G and see what happens to $Q$ while $S$ stays at 1.

items: (a)(i) Truth table for the exclusive-OR gate: $X = 0,\ Y = 0 \rightarrow Z = 0$; $X = 0,\ Y = 1 \rightarrow Z = 1$; $X = 1,\ Y = 0 \rightarrow Z = 1$; $X = 1,\ Y = 1 \rightarrow Z = 0$. The output $Z$ is 1 only when $X$ and $Y$ are different.

(a)(ii) The $Q$ state is an input to gate H, so the output of gate H is always 1 regardless of the state of $R$. The output of gate H is fed into gate G together with $S$; with $S = 1$ and the output of H equal to 1, the output of G (which is $Q$) stays at 0. So the state of $Q$ remains unchanged unless the $S$ input is changed to 0, at which point $Q$ changes from 0 to 1.

content.text: (a)(i) The symbol has a curved input edge plus a second, parallel curved line, which identifies an exclusive-OR (XOR) gate. XOR is 1 whenever exactly one of its two inputs is 1.

items: $X = 0,\ Y = 0 \;\rightarrow\; Z = 0$
$X = 0,\ Y = 1 \;\rightarrow\; Z = 1$
$X = 1,\ Y = 0 \;\rightarrow\; Z = 1$
$X = 1,\ Y = 1 \;\rightarrow\; Z = 0$

content.text: Rows 2 and 3 both give $Z = 1$, while row 4 gives $Z = 0$ because both inputs are 1. Detecting that two binary values differ is exactly what allows a latched circuit to respond to a change.

(a)(ii) The circuit is a pair of cross-coupled NAND gates, which is a set–reset latch. The output of a NAND gate is 1 only when both of its inputs are 1. Given $Q = 0$, the two inputs to gate H are $Q = 0$ and $R = 1$, so the output of H is 1 whatever the state of $R$:

items: $Q = 0,\ R = 1 \;\rightarrow\;$ output from H $= 1$
$Q = 0,\ R = 0 \;\rightarrow\;$ output from H $= 1$

content.text: That output of 1 goes to gate G along with $S$. With $S = 1$, gate G has two inputs of 1, so its output $Q$ stays at 0 and the latch holds its state. If $S$ is changed to 0, gate G has inputs 0 and 1, so $Q$ changes from 0 to 1. Only that change of $S$ alters the stored state, which is precisely what allows the circuit to store one bit of data.

content.text: Contrast open-loop gain amplifiers and closed-loop gain amplifiers in terms of their function and circuit construction.
Two axes of contrast: circuit construction (is any part of the output returned to the input?) and function (what happens to the output when the inputs differ even slightly?).
Note what happens to the gain in each case. Open-loop gain is very large; negative feedback is the mechanism that brings it down to a known value.

Open-loop gain has no feedback, so any difference between the inputs swings the output to a supply rail, making it useful as a switch or comparator; closed-loop gain feeds part of the output back as negative feedback to reduce and control the gain.

Open-loop gain refers to an operational amplifier when no feedback is provided. Typically, the open-loop gain is of the order of $200\times 10^{3}$. Any difference in voltage between the inverting and non-inverting input will cause the output to swing to the supply rail voltage. Using an amplifier in this mode is useful if the amplifier is used as a switch or in a circuit that is comparing two voltages and a binary output is required. However, where the shape of the waveform is important then a closed-loop amplifier is required. This means that a portion of the output voltage is fed back to the input as negative feedback. The effect of negative feedback is to reduce the gain of the amplifier.

content.text: With reference to the diagram provided, explain why both analogue and digital circuits are used in audio systems.

Work along the block diagram from left to right and classify each block: which of the seven blocks must work with a continuously varying analogue signal, and which can only work once the signal has been converted to digits?
For the digital part of the chain the key advantage is not speed or cost — it is what happens to the information content of the signal when it is stored, copied, transmitted and reproduced.

The microphone and loudspeaker at the ends of the chain must be analogue, but once the signal has been converted by the analogue-to-digital converter it can be stored, reproduced and transmitted by the microprocessor without loss of information.

Audio systems must involve analogue signals. The value of using analogue circuit components, such as microphones and loudspeakers, is that the input and outputs must be analogue for humans to hear it. Although analogue circuits can perform signal processing including recording, amplification and reproduction, the value of converting the signal to a digital form (analogue–digital converter) is that in digital form it can be stored, reproduced and transmitted without loss of information. Developments in integrated circuits technology (miniaturisation, increased functionality) have allowed audio systems to be incorporated into a wide variety of communication systems such as TV, phones and internet.
